description: The universe at scale: its origin, its stars, its gravity and light, the strange objects at its extremes, and its far future. Descends into quantum mechanics.

concepts.title: Cosmos
concepts.summary: Everything, at a scale that makes questions feel both small and precious. Light arriving from the past, matter caught in the act of falling together, and a universe slowly spreading itself thin.

concepts.title: Big Bang
concepts.summary: Not an explosion in space but the expansion of space itself, from a state so hot and dense that ordinary matter couldn't exist. Everything since has been cooling, clumping, and complicating.

concepts.title: Afterglow
concepts.summary: The oldest light there is, released when the universe first cooled enough to be transparent. It still fills the sky as a faint microwave hum, and its tiny ripples became galaxies.

concepts.title: Expansion
concepts.summary: Distant galaxies recede, and the farther they are the faster they go. It isn't galaxies flying through space; the space between them is stretching, which carries their light to longer wavelengths.

concepts.title: Inflation
concepts.summary: A proposed burst of enormously fast expansion in the first fraction of a second. It would explain why the sky looks so even and why the universe is so flat, and it remains a working hypothesis.

concepts.title: Dark Matter
concepts.summary: Something that pulls with gravity but never gives off light. Galaxies spin too fast to hold together without it, so it seems to be the unseen scaffolding the visible universe is built on.

concepts.title: Dark Energy
concepts.summary: The name for whatever is making the expansion of the universe speed up. We measure its effect clearly and understand almost nothing about what it is.

concepts.title: Stars
concepts.summary: Gravity squeezes hydrogen until it fuses, and the pressure that results holds the star up for millions or billions of years. A star is a long argument between collapse and heat.

concepts.title: Star Stuff
concepts.summary: Hydrogen fuses to helium, and inside massive stars on to carbon, oxygen, silicon, and iron. The atoms in your body and in every chip were made in stars, then scattered when those stars died.

concepts.title: The Sun
concepts.summary: An ordinary star, close enough to matter. Its light, eight minutes old on arrival, drives weather, photosynthesis, and nearly every food chain, and it has burned steadily for about four and a half billion years.

concepts.title: Supernovae
concepts.summary: The death of a massive star, when its core collapses and the outer layers are thrown outward at a fraction of the speed of light. For a few weeks a single star can outshine its whole galaxy.

concepts.title: Neutron Stars
concepts.summary: What is left when a giant star's core collapses but stops short of a black hole: more than a sun's mass packed into a ball about the size of a city. A teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tons.

concepts.title: White Dwarfs
concepts.summary: The quiet end for stars like our Sun: the outer layers drift away and a hot, Earth-sized core remains, slowly cooling over trillions of years. Most stars will finish this way.

concepts.title: Exoplanets
concepts.summary: Planets around other stars, found by the faint dimming when they cross their sun or the tiny wobble they cause. Thousands are known, and they come in far more kinds than our own system suggested.

concepts.title: Pulsars
concepts.summary: Neutron stars that spin, sweeping a beam of radio waves past us like a lighthouse. Some tick so regularly that they rival the best atomic clocks.

concepts.title: Magnetars
concepts.summary: Neutron stars with magnetic fields a thousand trillion times stronger than Earth's. Their crusts crack in starquakes that release more energy in a moment than the Sun does in years.

concepts.title: Degenerate Matter
concepts.summary: Matter squeezed so hard that quantum rules, not heat, keep it from collapsing. No two identical particles may occupy the same state, and that stubbornness holds white dwarfs and neutron stars up.

concepts.title: Fusion
concepts.summary: Light nuclei pushed together until they merge, releasing energy because the result weighs slightly less than the parts. It powers every star, and building a small, controlled version on Earth is still an open engineering challenge.

concepts.title: Gravity
concepts.summary: The weakest of the forces, and the one that never cancels out. It pulls matter into stars and planets, bends the path of light, and over enough time arranges the whole universe into filaments and voids.

concepts.title: Galaxies
concepts.summary: Hundreds of billions of stars held together by gravity, wheeling around a shared center. Spiral, elliptical, irregular: shapes that come from how they formed and what they've collided with.

concepts.title: Milky Way
concepts.summary: Our own galaxy, a spiral of a few hundred billion stars with a supermassive black hole at its center. From inside it, all we see is a faint band of light across a dark sky.

concepts.title: Cosmic Web
concepts.summary: On the largest scales, galaxies aren't scattered evenly. They gather in long filaments around enormous voids, a web laid down by gravity acting on ripples from the early universe.

concepts.title: Spacetime
concepts.summary: Space and time joined into one four-dimensional fabric. Mass and energy bend it, and what we call gravity is objects following the straightest possible paths through the bend.

concepts.title: General Relativity
concepts.summary: Einstein's account of gravity as the curvature of spacetime. It predicts bending light, black holes, and ripples in space itself, and every test so far has agreed with it.

concepts.title: Time Dilation
concepts.summary: Clocks don't tick at one universal rate. Move fast, or sit deep in a gravitational field, and your time slows relative to someone else's. GPS satellites have to correct for it every day.

concepts.title: Orbits
concepts.summary: Falling and missing. An orbiting body is always falling toward what it circles but moving sideways fast enough that the ground curves away beneath it.

concepts.title: Tides
concepts.summary: The Moon pulls harder on the near side of Earth than the far side, and the difference stretches the oceans. Twice a day the whole sea rises and falls to a rhythm set two hundred thousand miles away.

concepts.title: Light
concepts.summary: The fastest thing there is, and still eight minutes old by the time it reaches us from the Sun. Light carries almost everything we know about the cosmos: what it's made of, how it moves, how far and how long ago.

concepts.title: Spectrum
concepts.summary: Visible light is one thin slice of a family that runs from radio waves to gamma rays. They're the same thing at different wavelengths, and each one shows us something the others can't.

concepts.title: Redshift
concepts.summary: Light from a receding source is stretched toward longer, redder wavelengths, the way a siren drops in pitch as it drives away. It's how we know the universe is expanding.

concepts.title: Photons
concepts.summary: Light comes in packets, each carrying a fixed amount of energy. A single photon can behave like a wave and like a particle, and that double life was where quantum mechanics began.

concepts.title: Quantum Mechanics
concepts.summary: The rules for the very small, where things come in discrete amounts and outcomes are probabilities. It's strange and it's the most precisely tested theory we have; nearly all modern electronics rests on it.

concepts.title: Uncertainty
concepts.summary: You can't know both where a particle is and how it's moving with unlimited precision. It isn't a flaw in the instruments; the two properties simply aren't both sharply defined at once.

concepts.title: Superposition
concepts.summary: Until it's measured, a quantum system can be in a combination of states at once. The combination isn't ignorance about which one it really is; it has measurable effects of its own.

concepts.title: Entanglement
concepts.summary: Two particles can share a single state, so that measuring one tells you about the other however far apart they are. Nothing is sent between them, and it's still one of the strangest things physics has confirmed.

concepts.title: Wave Function
concepts.summary: The mathematical object that holds everything a quantum system can be said to be. Its shape gives the probability of each possible result, and its evolution is smooth and perfectly predictable.

concepts.title: Measurement
concepts.summary: When you look, a spread of possibilities becomes one definite result. Why, and what counts as looking, is still argued about, and physicists disagree on what the answer would even look like.

concepts.title: Wave and Particle
concepts.summary: Electrons make interference patterns like waves but arrive in single, countable spots like particles. Neither picture is complete, and both are needed to describe what we actually see.

concepts.title: Black Holes
concepts.summary: A region where gravity is strong enough that nothing, not even light, gets out. It's less a thing than a boundary, and at that boundary gravity, quantum theory, and information all disagree about what happens.

concepts.title: Event Horizon
concepts.summary: The point of no return: the surface beyond which nothing can come back out. To someone falling through, nothing special happens there. To someone watching from far away, the faller seems to freeze.

concepts.title: Singularity
concepts.summary: The place where the equations of general relativity give infinite answers. It's usually read as a sign the theory has run out of road, and that something we don't yet understand takes over.

concepts.title: Hawking Radiation
concepts.summary: Quantum effects near the horizon should make a black hole glow faintly and slowly lose mass. It's never been observed, but it ties gravity, quantum theory, and heat together in one idea.

concepts.title: Information Paradox
concepts.summary: If a black hole evaporates, what happens to everything that fell in? Quantum theory says information can't be destroyed, yet the radiation seems to carry none. The tension is still unresolved.

concepts.title: Quasars
concepts.summary: Supermassive black holes feeding on gas so fiercely that the hot swirl around them outshines an entire galaxy. Some of the light we see from them left billions of years ago.

concepts.title: Gravitational Waves
concepts.summary: Ripples in spacetime, made when massive objects such as black holes or neutron stars merge. They were first detected in 2015, and they let us listen to events that give off no light at all.

concepts.title: Heat Death
concepts.summary: One long-range guess about the far future: stars burn out, gradients vanish, and the universe settles into an even, cold spread where nothing can do work. It's entropy's furthest horizon, and still an open question.

concepts.title: Equilibrium
concepts.summary: The state where nothing changes on average: temperatures equal, flows stopped. It's the most probable arrangement of any isolated system, and reaching it is what entropy increase means.

concepts.title: Boltzmann Brain
concepts.summary: A thought experiment: in an endless, equilibrium universe, random fluctuations would sometimes assemble a brain complete with false memories. It's mostly used as a test of which cosmological theories are reasonable.

concepts.title: Proton Decay
concepts.summary: Some theories say even ordinary matter isn't forever, and protons very slowly fall apart. None has ever been seen, and experiments have already shown the lifetime is many, many times the age of the universe.

concepts.title: Ultimate Fate
concepts.summary: Cold and empty, a big rip, a crunch, a bounce: the options depend on what dark energy does. Current measurements favor the quiet one, but the honest answer is that nobody knows.

concepts.title: Solar System
concepts.summary: One ordinary star and what it kept: eight planets, their moons, and a scatter of rock and ice, all condensed from a single spinning cloud of gas and dust about four and a half billion years ago.

concepts.title: Planets
concepts.summary: Worlds large enough to be round and to have cleared their neighborhoods. Rocky ones sit close to the Sun and gas giants far out, a split that follows from where the early disk was hot or cold.

concepts.title: The Moon
concepts.summary: Probably formed when a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth. It stabilizes Earth's tilt, raises the tides, and is the only other world humans have walked on.

concepts.title: Comets
concepts.summary: Dirty snowballs left over from the solar system's birth. Nearing the Sun they sprout glowing tails, and they may have delivered some of Earth's water.
